title: Quantum Dot Foundations: Confinement, Strain, and Electronic Structure

slides.title: Quantum Dot Foundations: Confinement, Strain, and Electronic Structure
slides.subtitle: Section 1 of 5 | 28 Minutes | Graduate Physics & EE Lecture Series
bullets: Section 1: Quantum dot foundations (confinement, strain, electronic structure, materials)
Section 2: How a quantum dot emits (radiative decay, phonons, dephasing, spectral lines)
Section 3: Single-photon signature (quantum optics, g^(2)(tau), antibunching, Hanbury Brown-Twiss)
Section 4: Cavity QED and Purcell enhancement (micropillars, photonic crystals, waveguides)
Section 5: Electrical injection and simulator implementation (transport, diodes, RT emitter)
slides.notes: Welcome to the lecture series on how semiconductor quantum dots emit single photons, bridging fundamental solid-state physics to full-stack device simulation. Today's two-hour lecture is divided into five modular 28-minute sections. Section 1 covers the essential foundations: how three-dimensional quantum confinement creates discrete atom-like energy levels, how epitaxial strain shifts band edges and lifts valence band degeneracies, and how heterostructure band alignments dictate carrier capture and thermal escape. In Section 2, we will explore the radiative transition itself, including spontaneous emission via Fermi's golden rule, carrier-phonon coupling via the independent boson model, and homogeneous dephasing. Section 3 investigates the non-classical nature of light, deriving the second-order intensity correlation function g^(2)(tau) and experimental photon antibunching. Section 4 examines cavity quantum electrodynamics, Purcell enhancement, and directional photon extraction into waveguides. Finally, Section 5 integrates all physical mechanisms into an electrically driven room-temperature single-photon emitter simulation, evaluating realistic device designs from epitaxy to optical output [Fox, Quantum Optics, ch. 8] [Bimberg et al., Quantum Dot Heterostructures, ch. 1] [Michler ed., Quantum Dots for Quantum Information Technologies (2017)]. Let us begin with the bulk semiconductor host materials.

slides.title: Semiconductors in One Slide: Bands, Direct Gap, and Effective Mass
slides.subtitle: Direct optical transitions and band curvature in III-V materials
bullets: Direct bandgap: conduction minimum and valence maximum align at k = 0 (Gamma point)
Optical dipole transitions conserve crystal momentum: photon momentum q_phot ~ 0
Effective mass approximation: band curvature yields m* = hbar^2 / (d^2 E / dk^2)
III-V binary semiconductors provide direct gaps: GaAs is 1.422 eV, InP is 1.353 eV at 300 K
Small electron effective mass in III-Vs produces large De Broglie wavelength and strong confinement

equations.caption: parabolic conduction band dispersion near the Gamma point
effective mass tensor inverse related to energy band curvature

slides.notes: A semiconductor's optical personality is governed by its band structure at the center of the Brillouin zone. In direct-gap semiconductors such as the III-V binaries GaAs and InP, the conduction band minimum and the valence band maximum occur at the same crystal momentum, the Gamma point k = 0. Because the momentum of an optical photon q = 2 pi / lambda is negligible compared to the Brillouin zone width pi / a, photon absorption and emission occur as vertical transitions conserving crystal momentum [Yu & Cardona, Fundamentals of Semiconductors, ch. 6]. In indirect semiconductors like silicon, optical transitions require phonon assistance to conserve momentum, making radiative recombination orders of magnitude slower. Expanding the energy dispersion E(k) quadratically around the band extremum gives the effective mass approximation, where the periodic crystal lattice potential is absorbed into an effective mass m* given by the reciprocal of the second derivative of E with respect to k. For GaAs, the room-temperature direct bandgap computed from fsim_core/materials.py is 1.4225 eV with m_e* = 0.067 m0; for InP, the direct gap is 1.3529 eV with m_e* = 0.0795 m0, evaluated using the Vurgaftman et al. (2001) parameterization (1.424 eV and 1.344 eV are the Ioffe reference targets in verify/verify_materials.py). These small effective masses produce large carrier de Broglie wavelengths, making III-V heterostructures the ideal host for quantum confinement.

slides.title: Excitons in Bulk: The Hydrogenic Model
slides.subtitle: Bound electron-hole pairs, effective Bohr radius, and binding energy
bullets: Optically excited electron and hole attract via screened Coulomb: V(r) = -e^2 / (4 pi eps_0 eps_r r)
Hydrogenic Wannier-Mott exciton: reduced mass mu = (m_e* m_h*) / (m_e* + m_h*)
Dielectric screening (eps_r ~ 12-13) greatly expands orbit and shrinks binding energy
Hydrogenic estimates (GaAs 4.6 meV/12.1 nm, InP 6.0 meV/9.6 nm); accepted: GaAs 4.2 meV/11.2 nm, InP 5.1 meV
Room temperature thermal energy (kT = 25.9 meV) easily ionizes bulk excitons

equations.caption: exciton effective Bohr radius, where a_0 = 0.0529 nm is the hydrogen Bohr radius
exciton Rydberg binding energy, where Ry = 13.606 eV

slides.notes: When a photon creates an electron-hole pair, the oppositely charged carriers experience an attractive Coulomb interaction screened by the surrounding semiconductor lattice. In semiconductors with high dielectric constants and small effective masses, the electron-hole pair forms a weakly bound, delocalized quasiparticle known as a Wannier-Mott exciton [Fox, Quantum Optics, ch. 4]. By analogy with the hydrogen atom, the relative motion is solved by replacing the reduced mass with mu = m_e* m_h* / (m_e* + m_h*) and the vacuum permittivity with eps_0 eps_r. Because the static dielectric constant eps_r is large (~12.9 in GaAs and ~12.5 in InP) and the reduced mass mu is small (~0.056 m0 in GaAs and ~0.069 m0 in InP), the effective Bohr radius a_B scales as eps_r / (mu / m0), expanding the exciton radius to 12.1 nm in GaAs and 9.6 nm in InP under the simple isotropic hydrogenic model. Conversely, the binding energy E_B scales as (mu / m0) / eps_r^2, giving 4.6 meV in GaAs and 6.0 meV in InP. Alongside these hydrogenic estimates, accepted experimental values [Yu & Cardona 2010, ch. 6] reflect slight polaron and band-nonparabolicity corrections: 4.2 meV and 11.2 nm for GaAs, and 5.1 meV for InP. Because these bulk binding energies are far smaller than the room-temperature thermal energy k_B T = 25.85 meV, bulk excitons thermally ionize almost instantaneously at 300 K. To maintain stable excitonic emission at elevated temperatures, external spatial confinement is mandatory [Bimberg et al., 1999].

slides.title: Quantum Confinement: The Particle in a 1D Box
slides.subtitle: De Broglie quantization and why 5 nanometers is the critical lengthscale
bullets: Confining a carrier to width L restricts wavevector to discrete values: k_n = n pi / L
Infinite well eigenenergies scale quadratically with quantum number: E_n = n^2 pi^2 hbar^2 / (2 m* L^2)
Energy spacing Delta E scales as 1 / (m* L^2): light carriers produce large level separation
InP electron (m* = 0.08 m0, L = 5 nm) ground energy E_1 = 188.0 meV
Confinement energy (188 meV) is 7.3 times room-temperature thermal energy k_B T (25.9 meV)
Nanometer dimensions are required to prevent thermal ionization and maintain discrete quantum states

equations.caption: quantized energy levels of a one-dimensional infinite potential well of width L

slides.notes: When the physical dimensions of a semiconductor crystal approach the de Broglie wavelength of the charge carriers, spatial confinement forces the continuous energy bands into discrete eigenvalues. The simplest textbook model is the one-dimensional infinite potential well of width L. Boundary conditions require the carrier wavefunction to vanish at the barrier interfaces, establishing standing de Broglie waves with wavevectors k_n = n pi / L. Substituting this into the parabolic dispersion relation yields quantized energy levels E_n = n^2 pi^2 hbar^2 / (2 m* L^2) [Fox, Quantum Optics, ch. 4]. Notice that the energy scale depends inversely on the effective mass and on the square of the confinement length L. Consider an electron in InP, where m* = 0.08 m0: at L = 5 nm, the ground-state confinement energy E_1 evaluates to exactly 188.0 meV using the repository constant hbar^2 / (2 m0) = 38.0998 meV nm^2 from fsim_core/dot_levels.py. Compare this to the thermal energy at room temperature T = 300 K, which is k_B T = 25.85 meV. The ratio E_1 / (k_B T) is approximately 7.3. This quantitative result explains why 5 nanometers is the magic lengthscale for semiconductor quantum dots: only at dimensions of 5 nm or below does quantum confinement provide sufficient energy separation to overcome thermal excitation at room temperature.

slides.title: Finite Quantum Well & BenDaniel-Duke Boundary Conditions
slides.subtitle: Wavefunction penetration, effective mass discontinuities, and bound state count
bullets: Real heterostructures have finite barrier depth V: wavefunctions evanescently penetrate barrier
Discontinuous mass across interface requires BenDaniel-Duke condition: (1/m*) dpsi/dz is continuous
Hermitian probability current conservation across heterointerfaces
Even states satisfy k tan(k a) = r kappa; odd states satisfy -k cot(k a) = r kappa
Symmetric 1D well always binds at least one state for any V > 0

equations.caption: secular transcendental equations where a = w/2, k = sqrt(2 m_in E)/hbar, kappa = sqrt(2 m_out (V-E))/hbar

figure.caption: Transcendental root-finding and bound state wavefunctions from fsim_core.dot_levels.finite_well_1d

slides.notes: In physical semiconductor heterostructures, potential barriers have finite heights V determined by conduction or valence band offsets. Consequently, carrier wavefunctions do not vanish abruptly at the heterointerface but decay exponentially into the barrier with decay constant kappa = sqrt(2 m_out* (V - E)) / hbar [Bimberg et al., 1999, ch. 3]. Furthermore, because the material composition changes abruptly across the heterointerface, the carrier effective mass jumps from m_in* inside the well to m_out* in the barrier. To ensure Hermiticity and continuity of the quantum probability current J = (hbar / 2 m* i) (psi* dpsi/dz - psi dpsi*/dz), the standard boundary condition is the BenDaniel-Duke matching rule: both the wavefunction psi(z) and the velocity-like quantity (1 / m*(z)) dpsi/dz must be continuous across the interface. Matching even and odd parity solutions yields the transcendental equations shown on the slide. A heavier barrier mass (m_out* > m_in*) pulls the wavefunction closer to the well and lowers the eigenenergy, whereas a lighter barrier mass raises it. Crucially, in a one-dimensional symmetric well, there is always at least one bound state for any positive potential V > 0. The figure demonstrates the numerical solution implemented in fsim_core/dot_levels.py via finite_well_1d, showing the roots and normalized wavefunctions for an electron well.

slides.title: Density of States: 3D to 0D and the 'Artificial Atom'
slides.subtitle: Freezing degrees of freedom concentrates optical oscillator strength
bullets: 3D Bulk: continuous parabolic dispersion yields smooth square-root DOS: g(E) ~ sqrt(E)
2D Quantum Well (1D confinement): in-plane continuum creates staircase DOS: sum Theta(E - E_n)
1D Quantum Wire (2D confinement): axial continuum produces inverse-root peaks: sum (E - E_n)^(-1/2)
0D Quantum Dot (3D confinement): completely discrete delta-function DOS: 2 sum delta(E - E_n)
Zero-dimensional density of states mimics isolated atomic orbitals: the 'artificial atom'

equations.caption: density of states of a 0D quantum dot, with factor of 2 accounting for spin degeneracy

figure.caption: Evolution of the electronic density of states from 3D continuum to discrete 0D delta peaks

slides.notes: The dimensionality of a semiconductor structure fundamentally dictates how available quantum states are distributed in energy. In three-dimensional bulk material, carriers are free to propagate in all three Cartesian directions, producing a smooth square-root energy dependence g_3D(E) = (1 / 2 pi^2) (2 m* / hbar^2)^(3/2) sqrt(E) [Coldren et al., Diode Lasers, ch. 4]. Confining carriers along one dimension (a 2D quantum well) breaks the spectrum into subbands; within each subband, in-plane motion yields a constant density of states, forming a cumulative staircase sum of Heaviside step functions. Confining carriers along two dimensions (a 1D quantum wire) leaves only a single propagation axis, producing van Hove singularities with an inverse square-root divergence (E - E_n)^(-1/2) at each subband edge. Finally, when spatial confinement is imposed along all three spatial dimensions in a quantum dot (0D), all translational degrees of freedom are eliminated. The density of states collapses entirely into a series of discrete, atom-like Dirac delta functions g_0D(E) = 2 sum delta(E - E_n). This discrete spectrum eliminates thermal carrier spreading over a continuum band, concentrating all optical oscillator strength into razor-sharp optical transitions. For this reason, semiconductor quantum dots are universally recognized as solid-state 'artificial atoms' [Bimberg et al., 1999] [Michler, 2017].

slides.title: Confinement Regimes: Weak vs Strong Confinement
slides.subtitle: Comparing dot dimensions L to the bulk exciton Bohr radius a_B

columns.heading: Weak Confinement (L >> a_B)
bullets: Dot size L is much larger than exciton Bohr radius a_B
Internal Coulomb attraction dominates over boundary confinement
Electron and hole orbit each other as an intact bulk exciton
Quantization acts only on exciton center-of-mass motion
Confinement energy shift scales as Delta E ~ hbar^2 pi^2 / (2 M_tot L^2)

columns.heading: Strong Confinement (L << a_B)
bullets: Dot dimensions L are comparable to or smaller than a_B
Kinetic confinement (~1/L^2) dwarfs Coulomb interaction (~1/L)
Electron and hole orbitals are determined independently by dot potential
Coulomb energy acts as a perturbative correction (E_bind ~ 15-25 meV)
InP and InAs self-assembled dots reside solidly in this strong regime

slides.notes: The physical behavior of an exciton inside a quantum dot depends decisively on the ratio between the dot spatial extent L and the bulk exciton Bohr radius a_B [Fox, Quantum Optics, ch. 5]. In the weak confinement regime, where dot dimensions exceed the Bohr radius (L >> a_B), the Coulomb attraction between electron and hole is strong enough to preserve the internal hydrogenic bound state. Here, the electron-hole relative coordinate is virtually unchanged from bulk, and spatial confinement acts merely to quantize the center-of-mass motion of the composite exciton with total mass M = m_e* + m_h*. In contrast, when the dot dimension is smaller than the Bohr radius (L <= a_B), the system enters the strong confinement regime [Bimberg et al., 1999, ch. 4]. In this regime, the single-particle kinetic confinement energy scales as 1/L^2, completely overwhelming the Coulomb potential which scales only as 1/L. Consequently, the electron and hole wavefunctions decouple into independent single-particle particle-in-a-box orbitals, psi_e(r) and psi_h(r), established by the dot geometry and potential offsets. The Coulomb interaction between them is reduced to a perturbative first-order energy correction. Self-assembled InAs dots (a_B ~ 30 nm, height ~3 nm, radius ~12 nm) and InP dots (a_B ~ 10 nm, height ~4 nm, radius ~10-12 nm) are both solidly in the strong confinement regime along the vertical z-axis and strong-to-intermediate regime in-plane.

slides.title: Separable 0D Model: Vertical Well x In-Plane Disk
slides.subtitle: Adiabatic decoupling, Bessel radial matching, and s/p shell structure
bullets: Self-assembled lens dots mapped to a separable cylindrical disk: H = H_z + H_r,phi
Adiabatic approximation: vertical motion E_z is fast; in-plane motion E_r is slow
In-plane well depth is reduced by vertical confinement: V_r = V - E_z
Radial solutions inside: Bessel function J_l(k r); outside: modified Bessel K_l(kappa r)
s-shell (l=0) is spin-degenerate (2); p-shell (l=1) has orbital momentum m_l = +-1 (degen=4)

equations.latex: \frac{k J_l'(k R)}{m_{in}^* J_l(k R)} = \frac{\kappa K_l'(\kappa R)}{m_{out}^* K_l(\kappa R)}
equations.caption: BenDaniel-Duke radial matching equation across disk boundary r = R

figure.caption: Radial eigenfunctions J_0/K_0 and J_1/K_1 and energy levels from fsim_core.dot_levels.finite_disk_2d

slides.notes: To model self-assembled quantum dots analytically while retaining rigorous physics, the repository module fsim_core/dot_levels.py employs an adiabatic separable disk approximation [Bimberg et al., 1999, ch. 4]. Because self-assembled dots are flat structures with large aspect ratios (height h ~ 3-5 nm compared to base radius R ~ 10-15 nm), the vertical confinement along z is much stronger than in-plane confinement. Under the adiabatic approximation, the 3D Schrödinger equation separates into a vertical 1D finite well of width h yielding energy E_z, and an in-plane 2D circular well of radius R whose effective barrier depth is the remaining confinement V_r = V - E_z. This adiabatic depth reduction guarantees that the total energy E = E_z + E_r can never exceed the barrier height V, ensuring that escape barriers remain strictly non-negative. For circular in-plane symmetry, the angular solution is exp(i l phi), where l is the azimuthal orbital quantum number. The radial wavefunction inside the disk is given by regular Bessel functions J_l(k r), while the evanescent barrier tail is given by modified Bessel functions of the second kind K_l(kappa r). Boundary matching with BenDaniel-Duke mass continuity yields the secular equation shown on the slide. The ground state is the s-shell (l=0), which has two-fold spin degeneracy. The first excited state is the p-shell (l=1, m_l = +-1), which carries four-fold degeneracy (two orbital states times two spins), separated by an s-p shell splitting Delta E_sp ~ 20-35 meV.

slides.title: Effective-Mass Approximation & k.p Perturbation Theory
slides.subtitle: Multiband coupling, valence band mixing, and the limits of single-band models
bullets: Single-band envelope function approximation assumes parabolic, uncoupled bands near Gamma
Breaks down for deep confinement, sharp monolayer interfaces, and degenerate valence bands
k.p perturbation theory treats Kane matrix elements P = -i(hbar/m0) <s|p_x|x> perturbatively
8-band Kane model couples Gamma_6 conduction band with Gamma_8 (HH/LH) and Gamma_7 (SO) valence bands
At non-zero in-plane momentum k_t != 0, off-diagonal terms mix heavy and light hole states strongly
HH-LH band mixing causes band non-parabolicity and mass inversion away from the zone center

equations.latex: \mathcal{H}_{kp} = \frac{p^2}{2 m_0} + V_0(r) + \frac{\hbar^2 k^2}{2 m_0} + \frac{\hbar}{m_0} k \cdot p + \frac{\hbar}{4 m_0^2 c^2} (\nabla V_0 \times p) \cdot \sigma
equations.caption: k.p Hamiltonian for cell-periodic Bloch functions including free-electron term, k.p perturbation, and spin-orbit interaction

slides.notes: The single-band effective-mass approximation treats the electron and hole as simple scalar particles moving in parabolic bands. While computationally efficient, this picture has distinct physical limitations [Yu & Cardona, Fundamentals of Semiconductors, ch. 2]. Near the valence band edge, zincblende III-V semiconductors possess fourfold degeneracy at k = 0 between the heavy-hole (J = 3/2, m_j = +-3/2) and light-hole (J = 3/2, m_j = +-1/2) bands, with the split-off band (J = 1/2, m_j = +-1/2) separated by spin-orbit energy delta_so. Under k.p perturbation theory, the total crystal wavefunction is expanded in terms of zone-center cell-periodic Bloch functions. Coupling between the Gamma_6 conduction band and the Gamma_8 valence bands is mediated by the Kane momentum matrix element P = -i (hbar / m0) <s|p_x|x> [Chuang, Physics of Photonic Devices, ch. 4]. Away from the zone center (k_t != 0), off-diagonal terms in the 4x4 Luttinger-Kohn or 8x8 Kane Hamiltonian couple heavy-hole and light-hole envelopes. This valence band mixing causes pronounced non-parabolicity, anticrossings, and strong state-dependent anisotropy. In self-assembled quantum dots, single-band models capture the overall confinement scale to within tens of meV, but multiband k.p or atomistic tight-binding models are required to resolve fine details of hole polarization and wavefunction symmetry [Bimberg et al., 1999, ch. 4].

slides.title: Heterostructure Strain: Hydrostatic Shifts and Shear Splitting
slides.subtitle: Biaxial strain tensor, Pikus-Bir deformation potentials, and the Van de Walle sign convention
bullets: Lattice mismatch f = (a_sub - a_layer) / a_layer produces biaxial strain eps_xx = eps_yy = f
Poisson effect induces perpendicular strain: eps_zz = -2 (C12 / C11) eps_par
Hydrostatic strain tr(eps) shifts bandgap: dE_c = a_c tr(eps) and dE_av = a_v tr(eps)
Tetragonal shear strain Q = b (eps_zz - eps_par) breaks cubic symmetry and splits HH from LH
Compressive strain lifts heavy holes above light holes; LH-SO mixing saturates splitting at 2Delta_so/3 = 72 meV
InP on GaAs has f = -3.7%; on GaAs0.6P0.4 f = -5.1% (stronger compression and larger shift)

equations.caption: elastic tensor relations for pseudomorphic (001) biaxial strain

equations.latex: \Delta E_c = a_c \mathrm{tr}(\varepsilon), \quad \Delta E_{hh} = a_v \mathrm{tr}(\varepsilon) - Q, \quad Q = b (\varepsilon_{zz} - \varepsilon_\parallel)
equations.caption: hydrostatic and Pikus-Bir shear energy shifts of conduction and heavy-hole band edges

figure.caption: Band edge energy shifts and HH-LH splitting vs strain from fsim_core.materials.strain_shifts

slides.notes: Epitaxial growth on a lattice-mismatched substrate establishes pseudomorphic biaxial strain [Van de Walle, PRB 39, 1871 (1989)]. In-plane compression (f < 0) induces perpendicular expansion eps_zz = -2 (C12 / C11) eps_par via Poisson deformation. This decomposes into hydrostatic strain tr(eps) = 2 eps_par + eps_zz and axial shear Q = b (eps_zz - eps_par). Under compression, Q < 0. The small-strain linear formula Delta E_HH-LH = -2Q would predict unphysical splittings of 311 meV on GaAs and 428 meV on GaAs0.60P0.40. Because |Q| >> Delta_so (Delta_so = 108 meV for InP), the light-hole and spin-orbit bands mix strongly. As implemented in fsim_core/materials.py from Van de Walle's exact k=0 LH-SO block, the HH-LH splitting saturates at 2 Delta_so / 3 = 72 meV (evaluated to 71.96 meV at Q = -20 eV); evaluated values of 66.1 meV on GaAs and 67.8 meV on GaAs0.60P0.40 sit just below this ceiling. Crucially, the hydrostatic valence-band shift dE_av = a_v,VdW tr(eps) is negative: -19.7 meV on GaAs and -27.1 meV on GaAs0.6P0.4 (a_v,VdW = +0.6 eV, tr eps = -0.0328 / -0.0451). Hole bands move up entirely due to the shear term (-Q = +155.6 meV on GaAs, +213.9 meV on GaAs0.6P0.4), not the hydrostatic shift, yielding dE_hh = +186.8 meV and dE_lh = +119.1 meV on GaAs0.60P0.40.

slides.title: Critical Thickness & Stranski-Krastanov Island Growth
slides.subtitle: Matthews-Blakeslee dislocation equilibrium vs coherent 3D self-assembly
bullets: Elastic strain energy stored in a pseudomorphic layer scales linearly with thickness: E_strain ~ 2 G f^2 h
Matthews-Blakeslee model: beyond critical thickness h_c, dislocation formation becomes favorable
Critical thickness h_c is ~1.3 nm for InP/GaAs and ~0.6 nm (~2 ML) for InP/GaAs0.6P0.4
Stranski-Krastanov (SK) growth mode: 2D layer-by-layer growth transitions spontaneously to 3D islands
3D islands relax strain elastically along their free top facets without creating plastic dislocations
Leaves behind a thin 1-2 ML wetting layer (WL) that acts as a 2D carrier capture reservoir

equations.caption: Matthews-Blakeslee equilibrium critical thickness for 60-degree misfit dislocations, where b is Burgers vector

slides.notes: When an epitaxial film grows under lattice mismatch, elastic strain energy accumulates in proportion to the layer thickness h. In 1974, Matthews and Blakeslee derived the equilibrium mechanical force balance between the driving force of the misfit strain and the resisting line tension of a threading dislocation [Matthews & Blakeslee, J. Cryst. Growth 27, 118 (1974)]. Above a critical thickness h_c, generating plastic misfit dislocations becomes energetically favorable to relieve strain. For InP on GaAs (f = -3.69%), the single-layer Matthews-Blakeslee critical thickness evaluated by fsim_core/materials.py is h_c = 1.28 nm; for InP on GaAs0.60P0.40 (f = -5.07%), h_c drops to 0.59 nm, corresponding to just two atomic monolayers. However, under molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) or metalorganic vapour-phase epitaxy (MOVPE), highly strained heteroepitaxy often bypasses planar dislocation relaxation through the Stranski-Krastanov (SK) growth mode [Bimberg et al., 1999, ch. 2]. Growth proceeds initially layer-by-layer for 1 to 2 monolayers, forming a planar 'wetting layer'. As strain energy accumulates, the system minimizes total free energy by spontaneously nucleating coherent three-dimensional nano-islands. These islands relax lattice strain elastically through their free facet edges without forming dislocations. The remaining wetting layer acts as a shallow 2D quantum well that efficiently collects injected carriers before transferring them into the dot.

slides.title: Band Alignment: Model-Solid Theory and Type-I vs Type-II
slides.subtitle: Natural band offsets, absolute energy reference, and spatial carrier overlap
bullets: Van de Walle model-solid theory establishes absolute valence band offsets (VBO) via atomic potentials
Conduction band offset (CBO) follows by adding the strained bandgap: Delta E_c = Delta E_g - Delta E_v
Type-I (straddling alignment): both electrons and holes are confined inside the dot; high optical overlap
Type-II (staggered alignment): one carrier is confined in dot, other in matrix; slow recombination
InP in GaAs0.60P0.40: Delta E_c=200 meV, dE_v,hh=213 meV; hole depth V_h=94 meV (to barrier LH)
InP in Ga0.51In0.49P on GaAs is Type-I: Delta E_c = 202 meV, Delta E_v = 303 meV (model-solid)

figure.caption: Strained band alignment diagrams for InP in GaAs0.60P0.40 and InP in GaInP on GaAs substrate

slides.notes: Determining how conduction and valence band edges line up across a heterointerface is central to device design. In 1989, Chris Van de Walle formulated model-solid theory, establishing an absolute energy reference by aligning electrostatic potentials of neutral atomic spheres [Van de Walle, PRB 39, 1871 (1989)]. This yields the unstrained valence band offset Delta E_v0; applying spin-orbit splitting delta_so and strain shifts yields the strained band edges. In a Type-I (straddling) alignment, the narrower-gap dot confines both electrons and holes, giving high spatial overlap and rapid radiative decay (tau_rad ~ 1 ns) [Bimberg et al., 1999]. In Type-II (staggered) alignment, one carrier is confined in the dot and the other in the matrix, drastically suppressing recombination. The module fsim_core/materials.py computes these alignments via materials.offsets. For InP in GaAs0.60P0.40 on GaAs, materials.offsets yields a conduction offset Delta E_c = 200.3 meV (200 meV in dot_levels) and valence offsets dE_v_hh = 213.1 meV and dE_v_lh = 27.7 meV. Because tensile strain pushes the barrier light-hole edge 119 meV above heavy holes, the barrier LH is the topmost valence band. The effective hole confining depth is therefore V_h = E_hh,dot - E_lh,barrier = 93.8 meV (~94 meV). For InP in Ga0.51In0.49P on GaAs, model-solid alignment is also Type-I, with Delta E_c = 202.05 meV (~202 meV) and Delta E_v,hh = 303.10 meV (~303 meV).

slides.title: The Materials Question: Literal Cladding vs Workable Heterostructure
slides.subtitle: Why 'InP cladding / GaAsP active' is unphysical, and how (Al,Ga)InP resolves it

columns.heading: Literal InP Cladding / GaAsP Well (Fails)
bullets: InP bulk bandgap is 1.353 eV (1.3529 eV) at 300 K (cutoff lambda = 916 nm)
InP/GaAsP dot emits at 750-816 nm (photon energy 1.52 - 1.65 eV)
Photon energy exceeds InP bandgap: cladding is completely OPAQUE and absorbs emission!
InP lattice constant is 5.870 A vs GaAs substrate 5.653 A (-3.69% mismatch)
Thick (> 1 um) InP cladding relaxes with catastrophic misfit dislocation density

columns.heading: Workable Heterostructure Stack (Succeeds)
bullets: Active region: InP quantum dots in a thin, strain-balanced GaAs0.60P0.40 well
Cladding: (Al0.50Ga0.50)0.51In0.49P core and (Al0.70Ga0.30)0.51In0.49P outer cladding
Ga0.51In0.49P lattice matches GaAs substrate: a = 5.656 A vs 5.653 A (mismatch < 0.05%)
AlGaInP bandgaps (indirect X-min 2.25-2.26 eV, Gamma 2.26-2.39 eV) are transparent to 750-816 nm
Provides both optical waveguiding contrast and high electrical injection barriers

slides.notes: A fundamental engineering problem in this project is the materials paradox of designing a room-temperature edge-emitting single-photon diode [docs/rt_edge_tier.md]. A naive reading might suggest using bulk InP cladding layers surrounding a GaAsP active region. Solid-state optics rules this out completely: from fsim_core/materials.py, the 300 K bulk bandgap of InP is 1.3529 eV (absorption edge at 916 nm). Because the InP/GaAsP dot emits between 750 nm and 816 nm (1.52 eV to 1.65 eV), literal InP claddings would absorb 100% of emitted photons. Furthermore, InP has a lattice constant of 5.8697 A compared to 5.6533 A for GaAs (-3.69% mismatch), so micron-thick InP claddings would exceed critical thickness and generate dense dislocations. The workable solution implemented in cards/edge-inp-gaasp-design.yaml embeds the dot in a GaAs0.60P0.40 well clad by (Al_x Ga_{1-x})0.51 In0.49 P quaternary alloys. While ternary Ga0.51In0.49P has a = 5.656 A closely matching GaAs (5.653 A), the quaternary claddings have lattice constants of 5.6602 A (x_Al = 0.50) and 5.6619 A (x_Al = 0.70), maintaining negligible residual mismatch (<0.16%). Although both the x_Al = 0.50 core (Eg_G = 2.256 eV, Eg_X = 2.247 eV) and x_Al = 0.70 outer cladding (Eg_G = 2.391 eV, Eg_X = 2.261 eV) are indirect per materials.is_direct, their large minimum bandgaps (> 2.24 eV) guarantee complete optical transparency and low-defect epitaxy.

slides.title: Dot Sizes and Energies: HKUST Experiment vs the 816 nm Solver
slides.subtitle: Gu et al. (2025) 750 nm observation, solver limits, and the documented 160 meV deviation
bullets: Gu et al. (Opt. Express 2025) report 4-7 nm InP dots emitting at 750-755 nm in GaAs0.65P0.35
Single-band solver: evaluates to 816 nm (design card) and 836 nm (Gu geometry)
Documented deviation: ~160 meV red-shift documented in verify/verify_dot_levels.py (deviation d-iv-a)
What the single-band model gets right: realistic confinement scales, size-shift derivatives, escape barriers
Model limits: single-band without k.p mixing; elastic relaxation lowers the gap and cannot explain blue-shift
Honest modeling: simulator uses the physical solver output rather than fitting an unmeasured parameter
slides.notes: A rigorous engineering lecture must confront discrepancies between theoretical models and real experimental devices. In a landmark 2025 paper, Gu and coworkers at HKUST reported epitaxial InP quantum dots embedded in GaAs0.65P0.35 wells on GaAs substrates [Gu et al., Opt. Express 33, 23732 (2025)]. Cross-sectional TEM revealed dot heights of 4 to 7 nm and diameters around 25 nm, with ensemble emission around 750 to 755 nm (1.64 to 1.65 eV). When the repository single-band separable disk solver (fsim_core/dot_levels.py) is run on Gu geometry at 300 K, it predicts 836 nm (1.484 eV); the design card at h = 4.0 nm in GaAs0.60P0.40 predicts 815.7 nm (1.520 eV). This ~160 meV discrepancy is tracked as a documented deviation in verify/verify_dot_levels.py (deviation d-iv-a) rather than hidden [docs/rt_edge_tier.md]. Crucially, partial elastic strain relaxation cannot explain this blue-shift: in compressively strained InP, relaxation lowers the bandgap toward unstrained bulk, creating a red-shift (materials.strain_shifts gives Eg_hh = 1.4368 eV at eps = -5.07% relaxing toward 1.3529 eV at eps = 0). As documented in verify/verify_dot_levels.py, the discrepancy arises because the coherent single-band disk model neglects multiband k.p mixing [Stier et al., PRB 59, 5688 (1999)] and 3D strain tensors [Grundmann et al., PRB 52, 11969 (1995)], compounded by alloy ordering and ensemble type-I/II mixing.

slides.title: Carrier Confinement Summary: Levels, Escape, and the Thermal Ceiling
slides.subtitle: Confinement energies E_e, E_h, escape barriers, and Arrhenius retention S(T)
bullets: InP/GaAsP0.4 preset (300 K): electron state E_e = 97 meV, hole state E_h = 31 meV
Carrier escape barriers: electron escape dE_e = 103 meV, hole escape dE_h = 63 meV
InP/GaInP preset (300 K): deeper well V_e=415 meV gives E_e=180 meV, dE_e=235 meV
Arrhenius thermal escape rate R_esc ~ nu_0 exp(-E_a / k_B T) competes directly with radiative decay
At 300 K, single-channel 50% retention needs E_a ~ 262 meV; second channel caps S <= 0.0154
InP/GaAsP retention S(300 K) collapses to ~0.0010 (0.000964), setting the room-temperature brightness ceiling

equations.latex: S(T) = \frac{1}{1 + a_{\mathrm{esc}} e^{-E_a / k_B T} + b_p e^{-E_b / k_B T}}
equations.caption: two-channel Arrhenius thermal retention factor from fsim_core.integrator.retention

figure.caption: Potential wells, bound states, and Arrhenius retention curves S(T) from fsim_core.dot_levels

slides.notes: We summarize the electronic eigenstate solutions computed by fsim_core/dot_levels.py for our two primary systems. For an InP dot in GaAs0.60P0.40 at 300 K (height 4.0 nm, radius 12.0 nm), potential depths are V_e = 200 meV and V_h = 94 meV. Single-particle confinement energies are E_e = 97 meV (83 meV vertical, 14 meV lateral) and E_h = 31 meV (23 meV vertical, 8 meV lateral), leaving escape barriers dE_e = 103 meV and dE_h = 63 meV. For the InP/Ga0.51In0.49P preset at 300 K, deeper conduction confinement (V_e = 415 meV) yields E_e = 180 meV and dE_e = 235 meV (at 5 K: 436 meV, 184 meV, and 251 meV). As temperature reaches 300 K (k_B T = 25.85 meV), carriers escape via phonon-assisted activation at rate R_esc ~ nu_0 exp(-E_a / k_B T) [Chatzarakis et al., Phys. Rev. Appl. 20, 034011 (2023)]. For InP/GaAsP, shallow barriers yield E_a = 83.8 meV, collapsing retention S(300 K) to 0.000964 (~0.0010 in fig_01_15). The deeper InP/GaInP system (E_a = 135.0 meV) retains S(300 K) = 0.004617 (~0.0046). With two-channel parameters (a_esc = 24873, b_p = 100, E_b = 11.6 meV), E_a = 150 meV still yields only S = 0.0072, and the second channel caps S at 0.0154 even as E_a -> infinity; achieving 50% single-channel retention would require E_a ~ 262 meV.

slides.title: Exciton in a Quantum Dot: The Gaussian Binding Formula
slides.subtitle: Coulomb expectation value, relative coordinate integration, and transition energy
bullets: In strong confinement, single-particle orbitals psi_e and psi_h are established by the potential well
Coulomb attraction enters as a first-order correction: E_bind = <psi_e psi_h | V_c | psi_e psi_h>
With Gaussian envelopes exp(-r^2 / l^2), relative coordinate rho has width L = sqrt(l_e^2 + l_h^2)
Integrating 2D density p(rho) = (2 rho / L^2) exp(-rho^2 / L^2) yields <1/rho> = sqrt(pi) / L
Closed-form binding formula: E_bind = (e^2 / (4 pi eps_0 eps_r)) * sqrt(pi) / sqrt(l_e^2 + l_h^2)
InP/GaAsP dot: e_r = 6.704 nm, h_r = 6.541 nm, eps_r = 12.5 yields E_bind = 21.798 meV

equations.caption: Gaussian variational exciton binding formula used in fsim_core.dot_levels._gauss_binding
neutral exciton optical emission energy

slides.notes: Once the single-particle confinement states are solved, we determine the optical transition energy by including the electron-hole Coulomb interaction. In the strong confinement regime, the single-particle orbitals are frozen, and the Coulomb energy is evaluated as an expectation value [Bimberg et al., 1999, ch. 4]. The repository module fsim_core/dot_levels.py uses an elegant analytical Gaussian variational formula derived in _gauss_binding. The in-plane electron and hole envelopes are characterized by effective Gaussian lateral radii l_e and l_h, where |psi|^2 ~ exp(-r^2 / l^2). The relative coordinate vector rho = r_e - r_h is itself Gaussian distributed with a combined variance L^2 = l_e^2 + l_h^2. Integrating the inverse Coulomb distance 1/rho against the two-dimensional radial probability density p(rho) = (2 rho / L^2) exp(-rho^2 / L^2) yields the closed-form result <1 / rho> = sqrt(pi) / L. Multiplying by the screened Coulomb prefactor gives E_bind = (e^2 / 4 pi eps_0 eps_r) * sqrt(pi) / sqrt(l_e^2 + l_h^2). For our primary InP/GaAsP dot, the rms lateral radii are e_r = 6.704 nm and h_r = 6.541 nm (with mean orbital parameter lv.l_xy_nm = 6.623 nm) with eps_r = 12.5, which evaluates to E_bind = 21.798 meV (~21.8 meV). The net exciton emission energy is E_X = E_g(strained) + E_e + E_h - E_bind = 1.414 eV + 0.097 eV + 0.031 eV - 0.022 eV = 1.520 eV (lambda = 815.7 nm).

slides.title: The Biexciton State: Binding Energy and Radiative Cascade
slides.subtitle: Two-exciton Coulomb correlation, Delta_XX spectral splitting, and single-photon filtering
bullets: Biexciton state |XX>: two electrons and two holes occupying the ground s-shell in spin-singlet pairs
Total biexciton energy: E(XX) = 2 E_X - Delta_XX, where Delta_XX is the biexciton binding energy
Delta_XX incorporates attractive electron-hole Coulomb and repulsive carrier-carrier exchange terms
Typical values: Delta_XX is 4-8 meV for InP (Beirne 4-6 meV [DR via Reischle], Bommer 7+-1 meV [V])
Radiative cascade: |XX> emits at h nu_XX = E_X - Delta_XX, then |X> decays to |0>
Spectral filtering: a narrow bandpass filter transmits E_X and rejects E_XX, enforcing single-photon emission

equations.caption: total energy of the biexciton state relative to the empty dot ground state |0>
cascade photon energies for XX -> X and X -> 0 transitions

figure.caption: Biexciton cascade ladder and spectral line separation Delta_XX used for single-photon filtering

slides.notes: When two electron-hole pairs occupy a quantum dot simultaneously, they form a biexciton state |XX> [Michler ed., 2017, ch. 2]. By the Pauli exclusion principle, two electrons occupy the ground s-shell in a spin-singlet (S = 0), and two heavy holes form a pseudospin singlet (J = 0). The total biexciton energy is E(XX) = 2 E_X - Delta_XX, where Delta_XX is the biexciton binding energy or spectral shift. Delta_XX balances electron-hole Coulomb attraction, carrier-carrier repulsion, and exchange-correlation effects. In self-assembled dots, Delta_XX is typically positive (bound biexciton). For InP/GaInP dots, the evidence ledger records Delta_XX = 4-6 meV from Beirne et al. [PRB 75, 195302 (2007); Reischle et al., Opt. Express 16, 12771 (2008)] and 7 +/- 1 meV from Bommer et al. [JAP 110, 063108 (2011)], while Chatzarakis-class dots exhibit 5.9 meV [DR] [Chatzarakis et al., PR Applied 20, 034011 (2023); fsim_core/presets.py]. Relaxation proceeds through a two-photon cascade: |XX> decays to |X>, emitting at h nu_XX = E_X - Delta_XX, after which |X> decays to the empty state |0> at h nu_X = E_X. Because the two photons differ by Delta_XX, a narrow bandpass filter around the exciton line rejects the biexciton photon, enforcing high single-photon purity.

slides.title: Charged Excitons (Trions): X+ and X- Dynamics
slides.subtitle: Coulomb shifts, spin-singlet pairing, and deterministic electrostatic charging control
bullets: Residual background doping can inject an uncompensated carrier into the dot before optical excitation
Trion X- (2e + 1h): electrons form singlet (S=0); trion X+ (1e + 2h): holes form singlet
Trion emission lines are spectrally shifted from neutral X by 1 to 6 meV via Coulomb interactions
Absence of fine-structure splitting: singlet pairing cancels isotropic electron-hole exchange interaction
Trions emit unpolarized or circularly polarized single photons without polarization-dependent beatings
Gate bias in a p-i-n diode tunes Fermi level to deterministically select neutral X, X-, or X+

equations.latex: E(X^-) = E_g^{\mathrm{str}} + E_e + E_h - 2 E_{eh} + E_{ee}
equations.caption: negative trion optical emission energy where recombination leaves one spectator electron

slides.notes: If an extra charge carrier resides in the quantum dot prior to excitation, the resulting optical complex is a charged exciton, commonly known as a trion [Bimberg et al., 1999, ch. 4] [Michler, 2017, ch. 3]. An extra electron forms a negative trion X- (two electrons and one hole), while an extra hole forms a positive trion X+ (one electron and two holes). Because the two identical carriers occupy the same spatial s-shell, the Pauli exclusion principle forces their spins into an antiparallel singlet state (S = 0 for the two electrons in X-, or J = 0 for the two heavy holes in X+). Trion emission occurs when one electron-hole pair recombines, ejecting a photon and leaving behind the single spectator carrier. Because the trion contains an additional carrier, extra Coulomb attraction and repulsion terms shift the emission energy by 1 to 6 meV relative to the neutral exciton X. A profoundly useful consequence of trion physics is the complete absence of fine-structure splitting. Because the two paired carriers form a spin singlet, the net electron-hole exchange interaction vanishes identically. Consequently, trion recombination produces an unpolarized singlet emission line, avoiding the polarization-dependent beatings that can complicate neutral exciton emission. In electrically driven devices, applying a DC gate bias across a p-i-n junction allows deterministic tuning of the quantum dot charging state through Coulomb blockade.

slides.title: Fine-Structure Splitting: Electron-Hole Exchange and Symmetry
slides.subtitle: Anisotropic exchange interaction, C_2v symmetry breaking, and polarization eigenstates
bullets: Electron spin s = 1/2 and heavy-hole pseudospin j_z = +-3/2 yield four exciton spin configurations
Dipole-active 'bright' states have total angular momentum projection J_z = +-1; 'dark' states have J_z = +-2
Ideal cylindrical symmetry (D_2d) leaves the bright states |+1> and |-1> degenerate (circular polarization)
Real self-assembled dots have structural elongation and C_2v interface anisotropy that break cylindrical symmetry
Anisotropic electron-hole exchange mixes |+1> and |-1> into orthogonal linear eigenstates: |X_x> and |X_y>
Delta_FSS = |E_x - E_y| is typically 5-50 ueV in InP dots and 10-100 ueV in InAs dots

equations.caption: linearly polarized bright exciton eigenstates along [110] and [1-10] crystal axes
fine-structure splitting between linearly polarized exciton components

slides.notes: The internal spin structure of the neutral exciton gives rise to fine-structure splitting (FSS), a crucial consideration in quantum dot optics [Bimberg et al., 1999, ch. 4] [Michler, 2017, ch. 2]. An s-shell electron with spin s = 1/2 and a heavy hole with pseudospin j_z = +-3/2 combine to form four spin configurations. The states with total angular momentum projection J_z = +-2 are optically inactive ('dark' excitons) because single-photon transitions cannot carry two units of angular momentum. The states with J_z = +-1 are optically active ('bright' excitons) and couple to left- and right-circularly polarized photons. In an ideal quantum dot with cylindrical symmetry, the |+1> and |-1> states are strictly degenerate. However, real self-assembled quantum dots deviate from perfect circular symmetry due to in-plane elongation along crystallographic axes ([110] versus [1-10]), piezoelectric strain fields, and the atomistic C_2v symmetry of zincblende interfaces. This symmetry reduction activates the anisotropic electron-hole exchange interaction H_exch, which mixes |+1> and |-1> into two orthogonal linearly polarized eigenstates, |X_x> and |X_y>. The resulting energy splitting Delta_FSS is typically 5 to 50 ueV in InP dots and 10 to 100 ueV in InAs dots. For single-photon sources, FSS simply means the emission consists of two closely spaced orthogonal linearly polarized lines, which does not degrade second-order intensity antibunching.

slides.title: Single-Dot Isolation: Density, Apertures, and Poisson Statistics
slides.subtitle: Restricting active area to achieve high single-quantum-dot fidelity (N = 0.377)
bullets: Stranski-Krastanov growth nucleates a random spatial ensemble with areal density n = 10^8 - 10^10 cm^-2
A submicron aperture of diameter d restricts collection area to A = pi d^2 / 4
Number of dots k under the aperture follows a Poisson distribution: P(k) = N^k e^(-N) / k!
Design card: n = 3e8 cm^-2, diameter d = 0.4 um yields N = 0.377 dots
Probabilities: P(0) = 68.6% (empty), P(1) = 25.9% (single QD), P(>=2) = 5.5% (multi-dot cluster)
Conditional single-dot purity: P(1 | k >= 1) = 82.3% of light-emitting devices isolate exactly ONE dot!

equations.caption: mean Poisson expectation of quantum dot count under an aperture of diameter d
conditional probability that an active light-emitting aperture contains strictly one dot

figure.caption: Poisson distribution at N = 0.377 and mean dot count vs aperture diameter from cards/edge-inp-gaasp-design.yaml

slides.notes: A practical quantum dot single-photon source must isolate a single quantum dot from an as-grown ensemble containing millions of dots across the wafer. Epitaxial Stranski-Krastanov growth produces a random spatial distribution with areal densities typically between 10^8 and 10^10 cm^-2 [Bimberg et al., 1999, ch. 2]. To isolate an individual emitter, a submicron aperture is fabricated in a top metal contact or mask layer. The number of dots k captured within the aperture area A follows a spatial Poisson distribution P(k) = N^k exp(-N) / k!, where the mean expectation is N = n_QD * A [cards/edge-inp-gaasp-design.yaml]. In our primary edge-emitter design card, low-density epitaxy targets n_QD = 3 x 10^8 cm^-2 and the aperture diameter is d = 0.4 um. This gives an aperture area of A = pi (0.2 um)^2 = 0.1257 um^2 = 1.257 x 10^-9 cm^2, resulting in a mean dot expectation of N = 0.377 dots. Under these statistics, 68.6% of apertures contain zero dots (P(0) = 0.686), 25.9% contain exactly one dot (P(1) = 0.259), and only 5.5% contain two or more dots. Crucially, when testing devices on a probe station, empty apertures do not emit light and are discarded. The conditional probability that an active, light-emitting aperture contains strictly one dot is P(1 | k >= 1) = P(1) / (1 - P(0)) = 0.2586 / 0.3141 = 82.33% (82.3%)! Combined with spectral filtering, this provides exceptional single-dot isolation.

slides.title: Deterministic Dot Engineering: Mesas, Masks, and Site Control
slides.subtitle: Nanofabrication techniques for addressing and integrating individual quantum dots
bullets: Etched micro-mesas: dry etching (ICP-RIE) forms isolated semiconductor pillars of diameter 0.5-2.0 um
Opaque shadow masks: electron-beam lithography patterns submicron apertures in metal films (Al/Au)
In-situ optical lithography: maps exact coordinates of pre-selected dots with ~50 nm accuracy
Deterministic cavity alignment: optical resonators etched precisely concentric with registered dots
Site-controlled nucleation: substrate nano-patterning (pyramidal recesses) triggers single-dot growth at fixed sites
Eliminates spatial Poisson randomness, enabling scalable arrays for quantum photonic integrated circuits
slides.notes: While random spatial isolation via shadow masks is effective for individual research devices, scalable quantum photonic integration demands deterministic positioning of single quantum dots [Michler ed., 2017, ch. 10]. Several sophisticated nanofabrication strategies have been developed to overcome Poisson positioning randomness. The most common physical method is etching deep micro-mesas or nanopillars through the active quantum dot layer using inductively coupled plasma reactive-ion etching (ICP-RIE), isolating single dots in defined optical pillars. A second approach uses metallic shadow masks with nanoscale apertures defined by electron-beam lithography. To deterministically integrate quantum dots into photonic cavities or waveguides, researchers developed in-situ optical lithography: a low-temperature micro-photoluminescence scan maps the precise spatial coordinates of a bright, high-purity single dot relative to global alignment marks with ~50 nm accuracy, followed by aligned electron-beam lithography to pattern a cavity exactly centered on the dot [Dousse et al., PRL 101, 267404 (2008)]. Finally, site-controlled epitaxy uses pre-patterned nano-holes or inverted pyramidal recesses etched into the substrate prior to growth. Surface diffusion guides adatoms into the bottom of each recess, nucleating exactly one quantum dot per site with predetermined spatial periodicity.

slides.title: Material Platform Comparison: InAs/GaAs vs InP/GaInP vs InP/GaAsP
slides.subtitle: Key physical parameters across the leading quantum dot single-photon platforms
slides.notes: To provide broad context, this table compares three leading quantum dot platforms: near-infrared InAs/GaAs, visible-red InP/GaInP, and far-red InP/GaAsP [verify/verify_dot_levels.py]. Each column evaluates lattice mismatch relative to its matrix host: -6.69% for InAs on GaAs, -3.642% for InP on Ga0.51In0.49P (materials.mismatch(InP, GaInP) = -3.642%, distinct from -3.69% on GaAs substrate), and -5.07% for InP on GaAs0.60P0.40. InAs/GaAs features deep conduction confinement (V_e ~ 500 meV), enabling operation up to 230 K with short-period superlattices (SSL) [Chatzarakis et al., 2023], but emits beyond peak silicon SPAD efficiency. InP dots in Ga0.51In0.49P emit in the red (650-750 nm), well matched to silicon SPADs, with hole escape barrier dE_h = 48.4 meV at 300 K (49.2 meV at 5 K) from dot_levels; the Bommer-class preset (InP/AlGaInP0.2/AlGaInP0.55) deepens this to 90.6 meV. Reischle et al. (2008) demonstrated pulsed single-photon emission at 80 K. Our primary candidate, InP in GaAs0.60P0.40, bridges these regimes (750-816 nm), maintaining transparency and silicon compatibility, but shallower conduction offset (V_e = 200 meV) gives electron escape dE_e = 103 meV and hole escape dE_h = 63 meV. High LO phonon energies (43.4 meV in InP vs 36.6 meV in GaAs) also shape dephasing across platforms.

slides.title: Section 1 Summary: The Physical Foundations
slides.subtitle: Synthesizing confinement, strain, band structure, and single-dot isolation
bullets: 3D quantum confinement creates discrete atom-like density of states, concentrating optical strength
Strong confinement regime decouples electron and hole; Coulomb acts as a ~22 meV binding correction
Compressive biaxial strain lifts HH-LH degeneracy by ~68 meV, ensuring a pure heavy-hole ground state
Model-solid theory confirms Type-I band alignment; (Al,Ga)InP claddings resolve the transparency paradox
Biexciton binding Delta_XX (4-8 meV) enables clean single-photon spectral filtering against multi-photon pulses
Submicron spatial apertures with low-density growth (N = 0.377) yield >82% single-dot device isolation
slides.notes: In this opening section, we have established the complete physical foundation of quantum dot single-photon emitters [Bimberg et al., 1999] [Michler ed., 2017]. We saw how spatial confinement along all three dimensions collapses the continuous band spectrum into discrete Dirac delta-function states, creating an 'artificial atom'. Because self-assembled dots reside in the strong confinement regime, the single-particle kinetic energies dominate, while the electron-hole Coulomb attraction acts perturbatively with a Gaussian binding energy of ~22 meV. Biaxial compressive strain from lattice mismatch (f = -3.7% to -5.1%) shifts the conduction band upward and induces a tetragonal shear splitting that pushes the heavy-hole band ~68 meV above the light-hole band, ensuring that the optically active ground state involves pure heavy holes with high in-plane dipole strength. We resolved the materials question of the device tier: literal InP claddings are opaque and dislocated, whereas lattice-matched (Al,Ga)InP quaternary claddings provide wide bandgaps, high optical transparency, and excellent waveguiding contrast. Finally, biexciton Coulomb correlation provides a 4 to 8 meV spectral shift Delta_XX (Beirne 4-6 meV [DR via Reischle 2008], Bommer 7 +/- 1 meV [V]), allowing narrow optical filtering to isolate single photons, while spatial apertures with mean expectation N = 0.377 guarantee that over 82% of light-emitting devices contain strictly one isolated quantum dot.

slides.title: Bridge to Section 2: How a Quantum Dot Emits
slides.subtitle: From stationary electronic eigenstates to dynamic light-matter interactions
bullets: Section 1 established stationary eigenstates: energy levels E_e, E_h, and exciton energy E_X
Section 2 question: How do discrete electronic states couple to the quantized radiation field?
Spontaneous emission dynamics: dipole matrix elements |d_cv|^2 and radiative lifetime tau_rad ~ 1 ns
Carrier-phonon coupling: acoustic phonon sidebands via the independent boson model and the ZPL
Temperature-dependent dephasing: how acoustic and LO phonons broaden emission linewidth Gamma(T)
The fundamental filter tradeoff: rejecting the biexciton vs transmission loss at room temperature
slides.notes: Having established the stationary electronic eigenstates, band alignments, strain fields, and exciton binding energies in Section 1, we are now fully prepared to examine the dynamic light-matter interaction in Section 2: 'How a quantum dot emits' [Fox, Quantum Optics, ch. 8] [Michler ed., 2017]. The central question changes from 'what are the energy levels?' to 'how quickly and with what spectral purity does the quantum dot radiate photons?' In Section 2, we will apply time-dependent perturbation theory and Fermi's golden rule to derive the spontaneous emission rate Gamma_rad and radiative lifetime tau_rad ~ 1 ns from the microscopic interband dipole matrix element d_cv. We will then examine how the localized carriers couple to the vibrating crystal lattice. Using the independent boson model, we will dissect the emission spectrum into a coherent zero-phonon line (ZPL) and broad acoustic phonon sidebands. We will explore how phonon scattering causes pure dephasing, broadening the homogeneous linewidth Gamma(T) from sub-microelectronvolts at cryogenic temperatures to tens of millielectronvolts at 300 K. Finally, we will analyze the critical filter tradeoff: narrow spectral filtering is essential to reject biexciton photons, but as the exciton linewidth broadens with temperature, filtering incurs severe transmission losses. Join us in Section 2 as we bridge quantum electronics to photon emission.
